intro: Four modules take you through the Active Directory skills an IT support technician uses: how AD DS is built and what it depends on, managing users, groups and OUs, Group Policy, and day-to-day operations and troubleshooting. Practice in the labs, including a simulated Active Directory Users and Computers console.

sources.title: Active Directory Domain Services overview (Microsoft Learn)

modules.title: Active Directory fundamentals
modules.summary: Understand what Active Directory Domain Services does, its building blocks and how it relates to DNS, Kerberos and Microsoft Entra ID.

blocks.p: Active Directory Domain Services (AD DS) is Microsoft's directory service. It stores information about users, computers, groups and other resources in one database and lets people sign in once (single sign-on) and get access to what they are allowed to use. A domain controller (DC) is a server that holds a copy of the directory and answers sign-in requests.

list: Authentication: proves who you are (Kerberos, with NTLM as fallback)
Authorization: decides what you can access (groups and permissions)

head: Term
What it is
rows: A boundary for administration and policy, named like corp.example.com
Domains that share a contiguous DNS namespace
One or more trees sharing a schema and the global catalog; the top security boundary
A container for organizing objects and applying policy or delegating control
A user, computer, group, printer, etc., with attributes

blocks.note: An OU is for organizing, delegating and applying policy. Security groups are for granting access. Do not use OUs to grant permissions.

blocks.p: DNS is essential: clients find domain controllers through DNS SRV records, so clients must use the domain's DNS servers (not a public one). Time matters too: Kerberos rejects tickets if a client's clock differs from the DC by more than 5 minutes.
Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD) is the cloud identity service. It is not the same as AD DS, but many organizations connect the two (hybrid identity) so one account works in both.

tips: Clients and servers must use the domain's DNS servers to find domain controllers.
A time difference over 5 minutes breaks Kerberos sign-in.
Remember: AD DS is on-premises; Entra ID is cloud. They are different, but often linked.
terms: A server that stores AD DS and authenticates users.
The top-level container sharing one schema and global catalog.
A container for organizing and delegating objects.
The ticket-based authentication protocol AD uses.
Protocol for querying and modifying directory data.
A partial, searchable copy of all objects in the forest.

slides.title: What AD DS provides
script: Active Directory keeps users, computers and groups in one place and lets people sign in once.

slides.title: Domain structure
script: Objects live in OUs inside domains, and domains live in a forest.

slides.title: Depends on DNS and time
bullets: Clock skew over 5 minutes breaks Kerberos
script: Two things quietly break AD: wrong DNS settings and clocks that are out of sync.

slides.title: AD DS versus Entra ID
script: Active Directory Domain Services runs on your servers. Microsoft Entra ID is the cloud service, and many companies connect the two.

modules.title: Users, groups and OUs
modules.summary: Create and manage accounts, choose the right group type and scope, and organize objects with OUs.

blocks.p: Most help desk work happens in Active Directory Users and Computers (ADUC) or with PowerShell.

blocks.note: Locked out and disabled are different. A lockout is automatic after too many bad passwords; a disabled account was turned off by an administrator.

head: Type
Purpose
rows: Used to assign permissions (and can be used for email)
Email lists only; cannot grant access

head: Scope
Can contain
Used to grant access in
rows: Users and groups from any domain in the forest
Users and groups from its own domain
Users and groups from any domain

blocks.p: A common best practice is AGDLP: put Accounts in Global groups, put those into Domain Local groups, and assign Permissions to the domain local group.

Design OUs around how you administer, for example by department, location or object type, and keep the structure simple. Delegation lets you give a team limited rights over an OU, such as resetting passwords for the Sales OU only, without making them Domain Admins.

list: Follow least privilege: grant only the rights needed
Keep admin accounts separate from everyday accounts
Disable (not delete) accounts of people who leave, move them to a holding OU, and delete after your retention period

tips: Assign permissions to groups, never to individual users.
Reset passwords only after verifying the caller's identity.
Moving a user to another OU can change which Group Policy applies to them.
terms: A group that can be given permissions.
Accounts in Global groups, in Domain Local groups, which receive Permissions.
Giving limited administrative rights over an OU.
Temporary block after too many failed sign-in attempts.
The pre-Windows 2000 sign-in name, such as jlopez.

slides.title: Everyday account work
script: The help desk spends most of its AD time creating accounts, unlocking them and resetting passwords.

slides.title: Group types and scopes
script: Security groups assign permissions. Scope decides who can be a member and where the group can be used.

slides.title: AGDLP
bullets: Permissions on the Domain Local group
script: AGDLP keeps permissions manageable. You change who is in a group instead of editing permissions.

slides.title: OUs and least privilege
script: Use OUs to organize and delegate, and give people only the rights they need.

modules.title: Group Policy
modules.summary: Understand how Group Policy Objects configure users and computers and how to troubleshoot what applies.

blocks.p: Group Policy applies settings to users and computers centrally: password rules, drive mappings, firewall settings, software restrictions, desktop wallpaper and more. A Group Policy Object (GPO) is a collection of settings that you link to a site, domain or OU. It has a Computer Configuration part (applied at startup) and a User Configuration part (applied at sign-in).

blocks.note: Group Policy is configured with the Group Policy Management Console (GPMC). Default refresh for clients is about every 90 minutes.

blocks.p: Policies apply in this order, and later ones win a conflict: Local, Site, Domain, OU (LSDOU). Within nested OUs, the closest OU applies last.

head: Setting
Effect
rows: The GPO cannot be overridden by lower-level GPOs
An OU ignores GPOs from higher levels (but not Enforced ones)
Limits a GPO to chosen users, computers or groups
Among GPOs on the same container, the lowest number is applied last and wins

cmds: Summary of policies applied to this user and computer
head: Tool
Use

list: Is the object in the OU the GPO is linked to?
Is the GPO linked and enabled?
Does security filtering include the user or computer?
Can the client reach a DC and SYSVOL (DNS and network problems break GPO)?
Has the client rebooted or refreshed, for settings that apply at startup?

tips: Many policy problems are really DNS or network problems: check connectivity to the DC first.
Test a new GPO on a small test OU before linking it widely.
Use gpresult to see what actually applied, not what you think applied.
terms: A set of policy settings that can be linked to a site, domain or OU.
Policy order: Local, Site, Domain, OU.
A link setting that stops lower GPOs overriding the policy.
Applying a GPO only to selected users, computers or groups.
The shared folder on DCs that stores policy files and scripts.
Command that shows which policies applied.

slides.title: Group Policy
bullets: GPOs linked to site, domain or OU
script: Group Policy lets you manage thousands of PCs from one place.

slides.title: Order of processing
script: Group Policy applies from the local policy outward to the OU, and the later setting wins.

slides.title: Controlling scope
script: Use these settings to control where a GPO applies.

slides.title: Troubleshooting
script: Refresh policy, check what applied, and remember that DNS or network problems often look like policy problems.

modules.title: Running AD safely
modules.summary: Keep AD healthy: replication, FSMO roles, backup, secure administration and the problems that reach the help desk.

blocks.p: Most organizations run at least two domain controllers. Changes made on one DC replicate to the others. Problems with DNS, time or network links cause replication failures. Useful checks: dcdiag (DC health), repadmin /replsummary (replication status) and nltest /dsgetdc:corp.example.com (which DC a client uses).

head: FSMO role
Scope
Job
rows: Time source, password changes and lockouts, GPO edits
Hands out pools of IDs for new objects

head: Symptom
Likely cause
Fix
rows: "The trust relationship between this workstation and the primary domain failed"
Computer account password out of sync
Rejoin the PC to the domain or reset the computer account
Old password saved on a phone, mapped drive or service
Find the source in the DC's security log (event 4740) and update the saved password
Sign-in is slow or fails after a change
Client using wrong DNS, time out of sync, or no DC reachable
Check DNS settings, time, and connectivity to the DC
DNS wrong, no network path, or lacking rights
Use the domain's DNS and an account allowed to join

list: Use separate admin accounts, and do not browse the web or read email with them
Limit membership of Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins and Schema Admins; use delegation instead
Require strong passwords and multifactor authentication where possible
Enable the AD Recycle Bin so deleted objects can be restored
Back up domain controllers (system state) regularly and test restores
Keep DCs patched, and physically and logically protected

tips: Never log into workstations with a domain admin account: credentials can be stolen from memory.
A user who keeps locking out usually has a saved old password somewhere.
If a restore is needed, the AD Recycle Bin is much easier than an authoritative restore from backup.
terms: Five special DC roles that a single DC performs.
Copying directory changes between domain controllers.
A computer's secure channel with the domain is broken.
Feature that lets you restore deleted AD objects.
Separating admin accounts by the systems they manage.
Tool that tests domain controller health.

slides.title: Keeping AD healthy
script: A healthy domain has more than one domain controller, working replication, correct DNS and synchronized clocks.

slides.title: The five FSMO roles
bullets: PDC Emulator, RID Master, Infrastructure Master
script: Five special roles are held by individual DCs. The PDC Emulator is the one you notice most, for time, lockouts and password changes.

slides.title: Common tickets
script: Most AD tickets fit a few patterns. Learn the cause behind each one.

slides.title: Secure administration
script: Keep privileged access small and separate, and make sure you can recover from mistakes.
